about.body: Security analysis with an AI agent, live performance and maintenance for Windows. The scan only reads; changes happen only when you confirm an action in a Windows dialog, and each one is journaled with what is needed to undo it.
about.title: About Vigil

accounts.adminsNote: Administrators can change anything on this computer, including other accounts and the security settings.
accounts.allClear: Nothing unusual in the accounts or in the sign-ins of the last {days} days.
accounts.disabledByVigil: Disabled by Vigil on {when}; History can undo it.
accounts.domainNote: This computer is joined to a domain; your organization manages its domain accounts.
accounts.failuresHidden: Failed sign-ins are in the Security log, which needs administrator rights.
accounts.noFailures: No failed sign-ins in this period.
accounts.note: Local accounts, who is an administrator, who is signed in now and the sign-ins Windows recorded, read live. Nothing changes until you confirm it.

accounts.truncated: Only the newest events of a very full log were read.
accounts.warn.builtinAdmin.text: {account} is the built-in Administrator account. Windows keeps it off because password-guessing tools always try it. Use your own administrator account and disable this one.
accounts.warn.builtinAdmin.title: The built-in Administrator account is on
accounts.warn.cleared.text: {account} cleared the Security log. That erases the record of sign-ins; intruders do it to hide their tracks. If you did not do it, treat this computer as possibly compromised.

accounts.warn.created.text: The account {account} was created by {by}. If you do not recognize it, disable it below.
accounts.warn.created.title: New account

accounts.warn.guessing.title: Someone is guessing passwords
accounts.warn.guessingLocal.text: {count} sign-ins failed at this computer itself. Account names tried: {names}. If it was not you or someone you know, someone may have tried to guess a password here.

accounts.warn.guest.text: The Guest account ({account}) lets people use this computer without an account of their own. Windows keeps it off; disable it unless you need it.

optimize.noDrives: No SSD or hard disk with a drive letter was reported.
optimize.noPlans: Windows did not list any power plan (Modern Standby PCs use power modes in Settings instead).
optimize.planBalanced: Balanced: full speed when needed, saves power when idle. Best for most PCs.

optimize.runScanServices: Run a scan to list the services that start automatically.

optimize.servicesCount.other: {count} non-Windows services start at every boot. Updaters and helpers you rarely use can start only when needed.

optimize.startupLive.other: {count} apps start when you sign in.

overview.emptyBody: A scan reads every process, service, driver, scheduled task, startup entry, installed program and browser extension, checks their digital signatures and recent security events, and tells you what to remove, what to turn off and what to review. Nothing is changed until you choose an action.
overview.headlineClean: The local rules found nothing alarming. Run the AI review for a second opinion.

overview.headlineCritical.other: {count} items show strong signs of malware. Review them first.

overview.headlineSuspicious.other: {count} items look suspicious and deserve a closer look.

perf.ioNote: I/O counts every read and write a process makes (disk, network and devices).
perf.memoryExtra: Standby memory is a cache, not waste: Windows hands it to any program that needs it. Committed memory close to its limit is what really slows a PC down.
perf.netExtra: Connections per process are on the Network page.
perf.netNote: Windows does not report bandwidth per process without a driver; the Network page lists every connection and the process that owns it.
perf.paused: Paused: the charts keep this moment
posture.about.autorun: Stops CDs, DVDs and other drives from starting a program by themselves when they are inserted.
posture.about.bitlocker: Encrypts the drives, so a lost or stolen computer does not give away your files.
posture.about.credential_guard: Isolates sign-in secrets with virtualization so malware cannot steal them. It exists on Enterprise and Education editions and is usually set by the organization.
posture.about.defender: Checks files and programs as they are opened, downloaded or run.
posture.about.defender_updates: The antivirus needs current definitions to recognize new threats.
posture.about.driver_blocklist: Blocks drivers with known flaws that attackers bring along to switch off security software.
posture.about.firewall: Blocks connections from the network that nobody asked for. It should be on for every kind of network.
posture.about.lsa: Stops other programs from reading passwords and tokens from the process that signs you in.
posture.about.memory_integrity: Keeps malicious code out of the core of Windows, even when a driver has a flaw.
posture.about.powershell2: An old PowerShell that skips the logging and protections of newer versions, which attackers use to hide what they run.
posture.about.rdp: Lets people sign in to this computer over the network. When it is on, Network Level Authentication (NLA) makes them sign in before a session starts.
posture.about.remote_registry: Lets the registry be read and changed over the network. Home and personal computers do not need it.
posture.about.secure_boot: Lets only trusted software start before Windows, so a rootkit cannot load first and hide.
posture.about.smartscreen: Warns before you run apps and files from the internet that are unknown or known to be malicious.
posture.about.smb1: An old file-sharing protocol that WannaCry and other worms spread through. Current Windows shares files with SMB 2 and 3.
posture.about.tpm: A chip that keeps encryption keys and checks that the computer started without tampering. BitLocker and Windows Hello use it.
posture.about.uac: Asks before a program makes changes that need administrator rights, on a dimmed screen that other programs cannot click.
posture.about.windows_update: Updates close the security holes that attackers use.
posture.adminNote: Some settings can only be read or changed with administrator rights. Restart Vigil as administrator to see and change them.
posture.lead: The Windows settings that protect the computer as a whole, read live. Vigil only offers changes that make the computer safer; you confirm each one, and History can undo it.
posture.note.afterRestart: It is turned on and starts working after the next restart.
posture.note.autorunDefault: Windows already ignores AutoRun on USB drives; CDs, DVDs and some other drives can still start a program when they are inserted.
posture.note.bitlockerAdmin: Restart Vigil as administrator to read the drives' encryption.
posture.note.bitlockerMissing: This edition or this computer offers neither BitLocker nor device encryption.
posture.note.dataDrives: The system drive is encrypted; these drives are not: {drives}.
posture.note.legacyBios: The computer starts in legacy BIOS mode. Secure Boot needs UEFI mode, which is changed in the firmware settings; the system drive may first need converting to GPT.
posture.note.lsaOldWindows: On this version of Windows it is turned on through a policy and locks itself in the firmware, so Vigil does not change it.
posture.note.memoryIntegrityOff: Turn it on in Windows Security. If a driver is incompatible, Windows Security names it and keeps memory integrity off until that driver is updated or removed.
posture.note.noUpdateRecord: No installed Windows update was found in the event log.
posture.note.otherAntivirus: Another antivirus protects this computer, so Microsoft Defender steps aside.
posture.note.rdpNoNla: Anyone who can reach this computer over the network gets its sign-in screen before signing in.
posture.note.secureBootOff: Secure Boot is turned on in the computer's firmware (UEFI) settings, not in Windows.
posture.note.smb1Client: The SMBv1 client driver is installed.
posture.note.suspended: The drive is encrypted, but its protection is suspended, often during an update. It resumes after a restart, or in BitLocker's settings.
posture.note.tpmAbsent: No TPM was found. On many computers it is turned on in the firmware settings (Intel PTT or AMD fTPM).
posture.note.tpmOld: TPM 1.2 works with BitLocker, but Windows 11 and many newer features need TPM 2.0.
posture.note.uacNoDimming: Other programs can see and click the prompt.
posture.note.uacSilent: Programs can make changes with administrator rights without you seeing a prompt.
posture.note.updateOld: Check for updates in Windows Update.
posture.scoreFormula: The percentage weighs each setting by how much it matters (1 to 3); a setting that is partly in place counts half. Settings that do not apply to this computer or could not be read are left out.
posture.scoreParts: {partial} partly in place, {off} not in place

posture.scoreTitle.one: {on} of {count} recommended setting is in place
posture.scoreTitle.other: {on} of {count} recommended settings are in place

programs.search: Search by name, publisher, version or folder
programs.summary: {shown} of {total} programs shown · {size} declared by their installers
protection.activeNote: Microsoft Defender has not dealt with this threat yet. Remove active threats applies its recommended action, usually quarantine.
protection.adminNote: Changing Microsoft Defender's settings, exclusions and threats needs administrator rights.
protection.exclusionsHidden: Only administrators can see the exclusions. Restart Vigil as administrator to review them.
protection.exclusionsNote: Microsoft Defender does not scan these. Malware often adds exclusions to hide; remove the ones you do not recognize.
protection.externalRunning: Started at {time} outside Vigil (Windows Security or a schedule), so its progress is not shown here.
protection.flagAnyFolder: Excluded by name: a program with this name is skipped wherever it runs from.
protection.flagExecutable: Programs or scripts of this type go unscanned.
protection.flagWritable: Any program can write to this folder, so malware can hide there.
protection.fullScanRequired: Microsoft Defender needs a full scan to finish cleaning something it found.
protection.lead: Microsoft Defender, read live: its protection settings, scans, the threats it found and what it is told to skip. Vigil only turns protection on, never off.
protection.noExclusions: No exclusions: Microsoft Defender scans everything.
protection.noThreats: Microsoft Defender has not recorded any threat.
protection.offlineNote: The offline scan restarts the computer right away and takes about 15 minutes. It finds malware that hides while Windows runs.
protection.passiveRealtime: Off while another antivirus protects the computer.
protection.resultAttention: Scan finished after {time}. Something needs your attention: a threat was not removed or the scan hit an error. See the threat history.
protection.resultClean: Scan finished after {time}. Nothing needs your attention.

protection.resultFound.one: Scan finished after {time}. Microsoft Defender found {count} threat; see the threat history.
protection.resultFound.other: Scan finished after {time}. Microsoft Defender found {count} threats; see the threat history.

protection.statusFullScan: Microsoft Defender asks for a full scan
protection.statusLook: Some protection settings deserve a look
protection.statusLookDetail: Protection works, but a setting below is off or an exclusion lets files go unscanned.
protection.statusOffDetail: No antivirus protects this computer in real time. Turn it on in Windows Security.
protection.statusOkDetail: Real-time protection is on and the security intelligence is up to date.
protection.statusOtherDetail: {names} is registered with Windows Security. Microsoft Defender then runs in passive mode: it can scan when asked, but its real-time protection stays off.
protection.statusOutdated: Security intelligence is out of date
protection.statusOutdatedDetail: Microsoft Defender may miss recent threats until it is updated.
protection.statusRealtimeOffDetail: Files are not checked when they are opened, downloaded or run. Turn it on below.
protection.statusThreatsDetail: Microsoft Defender found threats it has not dealt with yet. Remove them below or review them in Windows Security.
protection.statusUnavailableDetail: It may be removed, turned off by a policy or replaced by another antivirus.
protection.swBehaviorAbout: Watches what programs do and stops the ones that act like malware.
protection.swCfaAbout: Ransomware protection: only trusted programs may change files in Documents, Pictures and other protected folders. Some programs may need to be allowed first.
protection.swCloudAbout: Asks Microsoft's cloud service about new and suspicious files, which stops new threats much sooner. Information about those files is sent to Microsoft.
protection.swNetworkAbout: Blocks connections from any program to dangerous websites. Organizations usually set it; Windows Security has no switch for it.
protection.swPuaAbout: Blocks programs that install adware, cryptocurrency miners or other software you did not ask for.
protection.swRealtimeAbout: Checks files and programs as they are opened, downloaded or run.
protection.swSamplesAbout: Sends files that may be malware to Microsoft for analysis. Files likely to contain personal information are not sent without asking.
protection.swTamperAbout: Stops other programs, malware included, from changing Microsoft Defender's settings. Only Windows Security can change it.
quarantine.note: Quarantined files are stored masked, so they cannot run, in a folder only administrators can open. Restore puts the file back exactly where it was.
quarantine.scheduled: The original is removed at the next restart
rel.allClear: No problems were recorded in the last {days} days.

rel.bootNote: From power on until the desktop is ready and the startup work is done, as Windows measures it.

rel.dumpKept: The memory dump is still there.

rel.kind.powerButton: Switched off with the power button

settings.ai.modelsFound.other: {count} models found: choose one in the list.

settings.ai.noModels: The server answered but offers no usable model (Ollama cloud models are left out).
settings.ai.providerNote: Who reviews the findings for a second opinion.
settings.ai.refreshModelsTip: Ask the server which models it offers
settings.ai.sentAuto: The items are sent to the first available provider; you confirm before each scan.
settings.ai.sentTo: The items to review are sent to {destination}.
settings.ai.staysLocal: Your data stays on this computer.
settings.ai.title: AI review
settings.autoRefreshNote: Update the process list every second.
settings.dataDir: Scans, quarantine, backups and the action journal are stored in {path}.
settings.eventLogsNote: How far back the scan reads Windows event logs.
settings.languageNote: Findings and actions follow it at the next scan.
settings.restorePointNote: Offer one before the first change of each session.
settings.secretNote: Stored protected by Windows; never shown again.
settings.title: Settings
settings.virustotalNote: Look up the hashes of suspicious files (the files are not uploaded).
settings.watch.autostart: Start Vigil in the tray when I sign in
settings.watch.autostartNote: Adds Vigil to your startup apps, for your account only and without asking for administrator rights. You confirm the change, and History can undo it.
settings.watch.closeNote: Vigil can keep watching from its icon in the notification area.
settings.watch.closeTray: Keep Vigil watching in the tray
settings.watch.notifyEvents: Events in the Windows logs (threats found, logs cleared, new administrators)
settings.watch.notifyHooks: Registry hooks, drivers, the hosts file, DNS and proxy
settings.watch.notifyNote: Every alert is kept on the Alerts page; these choose which ones also show a Windows notification.
settings.watch.scanNote: Scans with the local rules only (no AI, no VirusTotal) and tells you what is new since the previous scan. It waits while the computer runs on battery, a full-screen program runs or the processor is busy. Started in the tray without administrator rights, it sees less.
settings.watch.title: Background watch
settings.watch.watching: Watch this computer in the background
settings.watch.watchingNote: Every minute Vigil compares startup apps, services, drivers, scheduled tasks, security settings, registry hooks, the hosts file and remote-access ports with what it saw before, and reads a few Windows logs. It only reads.
startup.adminNote: This entry applies to every user of this computer: turning it on or off needs administrator rights.

startup.bootTrend.one: Last start took {last}; average of {count} start: {average}.
startup.bootTrend.other: Last start took {last}; average of {count} starts: {average}.

startup.hostNote: This entry starts a Windows program that runs another file named in the command. Its publisher and signature would be that Windows program's, so they are not shown: read the command to see what really starts.

startup.impactDetail.one: {cpu} of processor time and {disk} read at the last start ({count} start measured)
startup.impactDetail.other: {cpu} of processor time and {disk} read at the last start ({count} starts measured)

startup.impactNeedsAdmin: Startup impact and start times are measured by Windows and readable only with administrator rights.
startup.impactNote: Impact, as Windows measured it at the last starts: High is over 1 s of processor time or 3 MB read from disk (or a start made 1 s slower), Medium over 300 ms or 300 KB, Low under both.
startup.missingNote: The program this entry starts was not found; it may have been uninstalled. Turning the entry off is harmless.
startup.note: Read live from Windows. Enable and Disable flip the same switch as Task Manager: nothing is deleted, and every change is recorded in History, where you can undo it.
startup.onceNote: Windows runs this entry once at the next sign-in and then deletes it, so it has no on/off switch.
startup.policyAdminNote: A policy sets this entry, so it has no on/off switch. Deleting it needs administrator rights.
startup.policyNote: A policy usually sets this entry, and it has no on/off switch. Deleting the value stops it at the next sign-in; History can put it back. A policy that still sets it may write it again.
startup.search: Search by name, publisher or command
storage.chooseHint: Choose a drive or folder and press Analyze.
storage.componentStoreNote: Removes copies of Windows files replaced by updates. Takes several minutes; afterwards older updates can no longer be uninstalled.
storage.diskCleanupNote: The Windows tool also removes previous Windows installations (Windows.old) and upgrade leftovers.
storage.hibernationHint: Hibernation file and power settings are in Optimize.
storage.looking: Looking for files you can delete…

storage.measured.one: {size} can be freed in {count} place. Nothing is deleted until you press Clean.
storage.measured.other: {size} can be freed in {count} places. Nothing is deleted until you press Clean.

storage.minAge.one: Only files older than {count} hour are deleted.
storage.minAge.other: Only files older than {count} hours are deleted.

storage.name: Name
storage.settingsNote: Storage Sense can delete temporary files and old downloads on a schedule.
system.basicAdapter: virtual or basic adapter (no dedicated memory)
system.healthNeedsAdmin: Temperature and wear need administrator rights.
system.reliabilityQuiet: No blue screens, unexpected shutdowns or program crashes in the last {days} days.
table.name: Name
tasks.actionEmail: Send an e-mail (no longer supported by Windows)
tasks.actionMessage: Show the message "{title}" (no longer supported by Windows)
tasks.adminNote: Changing or running scheduled tasks needs administrator rights.
tasks.hideMicrosoftTip: Tasks under \Microsoft\ belong to Windows. Vigil shows them but never changes them.
tasks.microsoftNote: This task belongs to Windows (\Microsoft\). Vigil shows it but does not change it; use Task Scheduler if you really need to.
tasks.missingNote: The program this task starts was not found; it may have been uninstalled. Disabling or deleting the task is harmless.
tasks.noTrigger: Only when started by hand or by a program
tasks.note: Read live from Task Scheduler. Enable, Disable and Delete are recorded in History, where you can undo them; Run starts the task now and cannot be undone. Tasks under \Microsoft\ belong to Windows and are only shown.
tasks.resultCtrlC: Ended with Ctrl+C or its window was closed
tasks.resultNotSignedIn: The user was not signed in
tasks.riskyLabel: Full rights from a writable folder
tasks.riskyTip: Runs with full rights (highest privileges or as SYSTEM) a file from a folder that standard users can change. Any program you run could replace that file and gain those rights.
tasks.search: Search by name, folder, author or program
tasks.trigConsoleConnect: On local connection to a user session
tasks.trigConsoleDisconnect: On local disconnection from a user session
tasks.trigRegistration: When the task is created or changed
tasks.trigRemoteConnect: On remote connection to a user session
tasks.trigRemoteDisconnect: On remote disconnection from a user session
updates.failuresNote: Grouped by update. Windows tries a failed update again on its own; one that later installed is marked.
updates.fromEvents: From the System log: the Windows Update service was not running, and Vigil does not start it to read its full history. Update history in Settings shows everything.

updates.hint.deferredText.one: New updates wait {count} day before they are offered. Organizations do this to test them first; security fixes arrive later as a result.
updates.hint.deferredText.other: New updates wait {count} days before they are offered. Organizations do this to test them first; security fixes arrive later as a result.

updates.hint.deferredTitle: Updates are deferred by a policy
updates.hint.disabledText: A policy turns automatic updates off or hides Windows Update. On a computer your organization manages this can be on purpose; at home it usually means a tweaking tool or malware changed it, and the computer misses security fixes.
updates.hint.disabledTitle: Updates are turned off by a policy

updates.hint.failingText.one: It failed {count} time (last error {code}). Windows tries again on its own; if it keeps failing, the Windows Update troubleshooter in Settings or the update's own page with that error code usually tells what to do.
updates.hint.failingText.other: It failed {count} times (last error {code}). Windows tries again on its own; if it keeps failing, the Windows Update troubleshooter in Settings or the update's own page with that error code usually tells what to do.

updates.hint.managedText: A policy sends this computer to {server} for updates (WSUS). That is normal on a company computer; on a home computer nobody set up, it can keep updates from arriving.
updates.hint.managedTitle: Updates come from your organization's server

updates.hint.pausedText.one: For {count} more day (until {until}). Security fixes wait too; resume them in Settings when you can.
updates.hint.pausedText.other: For {count} more days (until {until}). Security fixes wait too; resume them in Settings when you can.

updates.hint.restartText.one: Installed updates take effect only after a restart, which has been pending for {count} day. Restart when it suits you.
updates.hint.restartText.other: Installed updates take effect only after a restart, which has been pending for {count} days. Restart when it suits you.

updates.hint.restartTitle: A restart has been waiting for days
updates.hint.serviceText: Without it no update arrives, security fixes included. Set it back to Manual in the Services page or remove the tool that disabled it.
updates.hint.serviceTitle: The Windows Update service is disabled

updates.hint.staleText.one: The last successful install was {count} day ago. Windows normally installs security fixes every month; open Windows Update to see what it is waiting for.
updates.hint.staleText.other: The last successful install was {count} days ago. Windows normally installs security fixes every month; open Windows Update to see what it is waiting for.

updates.hint.staleTitle: No update installed for a while
updates.historyUnreadable: The history could not be read.
updates.note: What Windows Update recorded on this computer. Vigil only reads it: it never searches for updates, and never downloads, installs or restarts anything.
updates.policyNote: Set by your organization, or by a program that changed them. Change them in Group Policy or ask whoever manages this computer.
updates.rebootRename: files a program replaces at restart
updates.standardUser: Running without administrator rights: everything on this page is readable, and nothing here needs them.
updates.statusRestart: A restart is needed to finish installing updates

watch.auto.found.one: Last automatic scan {when}: {count} finding to look at.
watch.auto.found.other: Last automatic scan {when}: {count} findings to look at.

watch.auto.interrupted: The last automatic scan stopped because Vigil was closed.
watch.auto.partial: It ran without administrator rights, so it saw less.
watch.auto.reason.fullscreen: a full-screen program or presentation is on
watch.logsNeedAdmin: Some Windows logs can be read only as administrator and are not watched now: {logs}.
watch.nothingYet: No changes noticed. Every minute Vigil compares startup apps, services, drivers, scheduled tasks, security settings, registry hooks, the hosts file and remote-access ports, and reads a few Windows logs.
watch.tasksNeedAdmin: Scheduled tasks are watched only while Vigil runs as administrator.
watch.title: Background watch
